explanations.explanation: Paul says that before their very eyes, "Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified." That's the picture he wants them looking at. I can relate, friend. My stamp used to come out like a smudge, and this picture was NOT a smudge. Paul points them straight back to the cross.

Moses, Israel's leader, never comes up in these verses. What Paul says was portrayed before their very eyes is "Jesus Christ as crucified." I get the guess, since the law is all over this passage. But the picture Paul holds up is the cross, not the mountain.

Abraham does show up later in this passage, but not for that. His offering of Isaac, his son, is told in Genesis 22, and Paul doesn't bring it up here. The thing portrayed before the Galatians' eyes is "Jesus Christ as crucified." Keep that one on the counter, baker.

Paul asks if they received the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith. He's steering them toward hearing with faith. I think he already knows the answer, but he wants the Galatians to say it themselves. It's like asking a friend who ate the last cookie while crumbs sit on their shirt.

Paul sets the two choices side by side: works of the law, or hearing with faith. He's pointing them toward hearing with faith, and the verses after it go on to say Abraham believed God (Galatians 3:6). So this one is true. Paul isn't leaning toward works at all.

explanations.answer: They changed course from how they began
explanations.explanation: Paul says they started in the Spirit and now are finishing in the flesh. That's a change of direction from how they began. It's like starting a batch with the oven preheated and then finishing it on the countertop. Paul's question shows the turn they made.

explanations.answer: They are moving too slowly to finish
explanations.explanation: Paul never talks about speed here. His words are about where they started and where they're finishing: "After starting in the Spirit, are you now finishing in the flesh?" The problem he points to is the direction they went. Nobody's behind schedule, baker.

explanations.answer: They should start over under the law
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Paul says. He asks, "Are you so foolish?" about finishing in the flesh after starting in the Spirit. He never tells them to go back to the starting line under the law. His question points at the change they already made.

Paul says God lavishes His Spirit on them and works miracles among them. Then he asks if that's because they practice the law, or because they hear and believe. The word lavish is a big one, friend. It's more generous than me with the sprinkles on a birthday batch.

Paul doesn't mention prophets in these verses. He says God "lavish[es] His Spirit" on them and works miracles among them. The question he asks is whether that comes from practicing the law or from hearing and believing. Keep your eyes on the miracles, baker.

Visions don't show up in Paul's question. He says God lavishes His Spirit on them and works miracles among them. Then he asks whether the law or hearing with faith is behind it. The answer in the verse is miracles.

"Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." Paul quotes this line to show where Abraham's righteousness came from. It was credited to him because he believed. That's a gift on the counter, friend, not a paycheck.

Close to the neighborhood, but that's not the word Paul quotes. The line he picks is "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." His whole point in this part is about faith. Believed is the word in the verse.
Fear isn't the word here, baker. Paul quotes, "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." The word that does the work is believed. It was credited to him as righteousness.

Paul says it plainly: "those who have faith are sons of Abraham." Since Abraham believed God, the ones who share that faith are counted as his sons. It's a family table with a very big seat count. Nobody's checking a family tree at the door.

explanations.answer: Those born in his family line
explanations.explanation: That's not how Paul says it. He writes, "those who have faith are sons of Abraham." Family line isn't the test in this verse. Faith is, friend.

Paul goes the other way. He says "those who have faith are sons of Abraham." Then in verse 10 he says all who rely on works of the law are under a curse. So faith is what he points to here, not the law.

"All nations will be blessed through you." Paul says the Scripture foretold the gospel to Abraham in those words. He calls it the gospel, and he says it was told ahead of time. That's a very big batch, friend. Every nation gets a box.

Tribes sounds close, but that's not the word. Paul quotes the promise to Abraham as "All nations will be blessed through you." He's talking about the Gentiles, which means the nations. The word is nations, baker.
Kings isn't in the promise. Paul quotes it this way: "All nations will be blessed through you." That's a much wider circle than a few royal guests. The blessing goes to nations.
Paul says, "All who rely on works of the law are under a curse." That's a hard sentence. I won't dress it up with sprinkles. It's the setup for what he says about Christ in verse 13.
Burden is a fair word, but it isn't the one Paul uses. He says, "All who rely on works of the law are under a curse." That's heavier than a burden. I think that's why the next verses matter so much.
Shadow isn't in the verse, friend. Paul writes, "All who rely on works of the law are under a curse." It's a strong word on purpose. The right word is curse.

Paul quotes, "Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law." That's every line, every time. I can't get through one batch without dropping a chocolate chip, so I feel that one. Paul's point is that relying on the law means relying on everything.

Most of it doesn't make the cut in this verse. Paul quotes, "Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law." The word is everything. There's no passing grade in that line, baker.

The verse doesn't pick out main parts. It says, "Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law." That covers all of it, not a highlight reel. The answer is everything.
"The righteous will live by faith." Paul says that right after saying no one is justified before God by the law. He's quoting Scripture to back it up. Faith is where the righteous live, friend.

Works is the opposite of the line Paul quotes. He says no one is justified before God by the law, because "The righteous will live by faith." So the word is faith. That's the verse that closes the case.
Sight isn't in this verse, baker. Paul quotes, "The righteous will live by faith." He uses it to show that no one is justified before God by the law. The word is faith.
Paul says the opposite. He writes, "The law, however, is not based on faith; on the contrary, 'The man who does these things will live by them.'" The law is about doing. So this one is false, friend.

Right, Paul says "The law, however, is not based on faith." He follows it with, "on the contrary, 'The man who does these things will live by them.'" The law is about doing. Faith is a different road.
Paul says, "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law." After a few heavy verses, this is the turn. The One who did it is Christ, plain and simple. I'm doing a little hop on my gold base, baker.
Moses, Israel's leader, isn't who Paul names here. He writes, "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law." The one who redeems is Christ. Moses doesn't appear anywhere in these verses.

Abraham is in this passage, but not as the one who redeems. Paul says the blessing was promised to him and that he's the man of faith (Galatians 3:9). The one who redeemed us from the curse of the law is Christ. That's verse 13.

explanations.answer: By becoming a curse for us
explanations.explanation: Paul writes, "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us." He backs it with Scripture: "Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree." I can't say much more than that, friend, except that this is the heart of it. Christ did it for us.

The temple tax isn't anywhere in these verses. Paul says Christ redeemed us "by becoming a curse for us." Then he quotes, "Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree." That's the way he says it happened.
That's a neat idea, but it's not what the verse says. Paul writes that Christ redeemed us "by becoming a curse for us." It's not a curse sent off somewhere. Christ took it on for us, baker.

Paul says Christ redeemed us "in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus." That's the reason he gives. The blessing promised to Abraham reaches the Gentiles in Christ Jesus. That includes a lot of us, friend.

This one is true. Paul writes, "He redeemed us in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus." That's the reason he gives in verse 14. The promise to Abraham reaches the Gentiles in Christ.

Paul says it's "so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit." That takes us back to the beginning, when he asked how they received the Spirit (Galatians 3:2). Faith, then and now. Funny how the end of the passage ties up like a good cookie box, friend.

Land isn't the word in this verse. Paul says Christ redeemed us so that "by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit." The promise here is the Spirit. Keep the boxes tied up with that one, baker.

Kingdom isn't what Paul writes here. He says it's "so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit." The word that finishes the sentence is Spirit. It also loops back to his question in verse 2.
